claim: The evolutionarily conserved catalytic glutamate 254 of α-tubulin was mutated to alanine (E254A) to generate a tubulin variant with blocked GTP hydrolysis.
source: We generated wildtype α/β-tubulin and a tubulin variant with blocked GTP hydrolysis by mutating the evolutionarily conserved catalytic glutamate 254 of α-tubulin (Nogales et al., 1998) to alanine (E254A) (Figure 1a–b, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing the mutation was made and by citation to prior work establishing the catalytic role of this residue.

claim: The E254A mutation is lethal in budding yeast because cell division fails due to loss of microtubule dynamics.
source: This mutation is lethal in budding yeast, as cell division fails due to loss of microtubule dynamics (Anders and Botstein, 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior published work.

claim: Wildtype human tubulin microtubules contain a 1:1 ratio of GTP:GDP.
source: We measured the GTP content of microtubules polymerized from purified recombinant human wildtype tubulin and tubulin purified from porcine brain as a control. We observed the expected 1:1 ratio of GTP:GDP (Figure 1c–d), since GTP is hydrolyzed only at its inter-tubulin dimer, but not at the intra-dimer binding site (Kobayashi, 1975).
evidence: The claim is supported by HPLC data shown in Figure 1c-d and by citation to prior work explaining the biochemical basis.

claim: E254A microtubules bind almost exclusively GTP, demonstrating that GTP hydrolysis is blocked in this mutant.
source: In contrast, E254A microtubules bound almost exclusively GTP (Figure 1c–d), demonstrating that GTP hydrolysis is indeed blocked in this mutant.
evidence: The claim is supported by HPLC data shown in Figure 1c-d measuring nucleotide content.

claim: Human wildtype microtubules grow dynamically, displaying occasional transitions to depolymerization (catastrophes).
source: In the presence of GTP, human wildtype microtubules grew dynamically (Figure 1e–f, Video 1) similarly to porcine brain microtubules (Figure 1—figure supplement 2b–c), displaying occasional transitions to depolymerization, called catastrophes, as expected (Vemu et al., 2017; Vemu et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by iSCAT microscopy data shown in Figure 1e-f and Video 1, and by citations to prior work.

claim: Wildtype tubulin hardly nucleates microtubules spontaneously.
source: Wildtype tubulin hardly nucleated any microtubules spontaneously (Figure 1g, Videos 1 and 2)
evidence: The claim is supported by iSCAT microscopy data shown in Figure 1g and Videos 1 and 2.

claim: E254A tubulin nucleates microtubules very efficiently even at low concentrations.
source: whereas E254A tubulin nucleated microtubules very efficiently even at low concentrations, quickly reaching high microtubule densities (Figure 1h, Video 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by iSCAT microscopy data shown in Figure 1h and Video 3.

claim: E254A mutant microtubules are hyper-stable for hours, never exhibiting catastrophes.
source: Moreover, these mutant microtubules were hyper-stable for hours, never exhibiting catastrophes.
evidence: The claim is supported by observational data from microscopy experiments.

claim: The properties of E254A microtubules are similar to the behavior of microtubules polymerized in the presence of the non-hydrolysable GTP analogue GMPCPP.
source: These properties agree with the anticipated behavior of hydrolysis-deficient microtubules, and are similar to the behavior of microtubules polymerized in the presence of the non-hydrolysable GTP analogue GMPCPP (Hyman et al., 1992).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison to prior published work on GMPCPP microtubules.

claim: EB3 binds to the growing plus and minus ends of wildtype microtubules in a comet-like manner.
source: Simultaneous total internal reflection fluorescence (TIRF) microscopy of mGFP-EB3 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a) and iSCAT imaging of unlabeled microtubules revealed that EB3 bound to the growing plus and minus ends of wildtype microtubules in the expected comet-like manner (Figure 2a–c, Video 4; Bieling et al., 2008; Bieling et al., 2007; Komarova et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by TIRF/iSCAT microscopy data shown in Figure 2a-c and Video 4, and by citations to prior work.

claim: The apparent dissociation constant for EB3 binding to growing wildtype microtubule ends is approximately 40 nM.
source: The apparent dissociation constant for binding to growing microtubule ends was ~40 nM (Figure 2d).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of EB3 binding data shown in Figure 2d.

claim: EB3 has no effect on wildtype microtubule growth speed.
source: EB3 had no effect on the wildtype microtubule growth speed (Figure 2e).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 2e.

claim: EB3 decorates the entire lattice of GTPase-deficient E254A mutant microtubules.
source: In clear contrast, EB3 decorated the entire lattice of GTPase-deficient E254A mutant microtubules (Figure 2f–h; Figure 2—figure supplement 1b), reminiscent of its binding to microtubules grown in the presence of the non-hydrolysable GTP analogue GTPγS (Maurer et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by TIRF microscopy data shown in Figure 2f-h and Figure 2—figure supplement 1b, and by citation to prior work.

claim: EB3 fails to bind human wildtype microtubules polymerized in the presence of GMPCPP.
source: However, EB3 failed to bind human wildtype microtubules polymerized in the presence of GMPCPP (Figure 2—figure supplement 1c), as observed previously with mammalian brain microtubules (Maurer et al., 2011; Roth et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by TIRF microscopy data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1c and by citations to prior work.

claim: The negative effect of GMPCPP on EB3 binding affinity is due to the bound nucleotide and not the E254A mutation itself.
source: This negative effect of GMPCPP on the EB3 binding affinity was also observed when E254A microtubules were grown in the presence of this GTP analogue (Figure 2—figure supplement 1d), demonstrating that it is indeed the bound nucleotide and not the single point mutation itself that controls the microtubule conformation and hence the affinity of EB3 binding.
evidence: The claim is supported by TIRF microscopy data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1d.

claim: The apparent dissociation constant for EB3 binding to E254A microtubules is approximately 8 nM.
source: With an apparent dissociation constant of ~8 nM (Figure 2i), EB3 binding to E254A microtubules was stronger than to growing wildtype ends (Figure 2d).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 2i and comparison to Figure 2d.

claim: Unbinding of mGFP-EB3 from E254A microtubules is very slow.
source: Unbinding of mGFP-EB3 from E254A microtubules was very slow (Figure 2j–k, Figure 2—figure supplement 1f–g).
evidence: The claim is supported by single molecule imaging data shown in Figure 2j-k and Figure 2—figure supplement 1f-g.

claim: EB3 displays strong affinity to microtubules locked in the GTP state, establishing it as a bona fide GTP cap marker.
source: Together these results show that EB3 displays strong affinity to microtubules locked in the GTP state, clearly establishing it as a bona fide GTP cap marker.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the experimental data on EB3 binding to E254A microtubules.

claim: E254A microtubules simultaneously capture properties that different GTP analogues induce separately in wildtype microtubules: strong microtubule nucleation as with GMPCPP, and high EB binding affinity as with GTPγS.
source: Interestingly, E254A microtubules simultaneously capture properties that different GTP analogues induce separately in wildtype microtubules: strong microtubule nucleation as in the presence of GMPCPP, and high EB binding affinity as in the presence of GTPγS (Hyman et al., 1992; Maurer et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of experimental data with prior published work on GTP analogues.

claim: TPX2micro displays higher affinity towards GMPCPP microtubules than towards growing microtubule ends.
source: Another protein that discriminates between a GMPCPP microtubule and a growing microtubule end is a short fragment of the multifunctional anti-catastrophe factor TPX2 (Wittmann et al., 2000), previously called TPX2micro (Zhang et al., 2017). Opposite to EBs, it displays higher affinity towards GMPCPP microtubules than towards growing microtubule ends (Zhang et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: TPX2micro binds poorly to E254A microtubules compared to GMPCPP microtubules.
source: We observed that this fragment also binds poorly to E254A microtubules compared to GMPCPP microtubules (Figure 2—figure supplement 1e), again suggesting that GTP-bound mutant microtubules are similar to growing microtubule ends.
evidence: The claim is supported by TIRF microscopy data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1e.

claim: Microtubules grown in GTP analogues display only partial aspects of the GTP conformation of microtubules.
source: These results suggest that microtubules grown in GTP analogues display only partial aspects of the GTP conformation of microtubules, which explains previous contradictory interpretations based on results obtained with such analogues.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the experimental data comparing E254A microtubules with GMPCPP and GTPγS microtubules.

claim: A GTP-containing E254A mutant microtubule is currently the best static mimic for the microtubule conformation in the transiently existing GTP cap.
source: In conclusion, a GTP-containing E254A mutant microtubule currently appears to be the best static mimic for the microtubule conformation in the only transiently existing GTP cap.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the experimental data comparing E254A microtubules with other GTP analogues.

claim: The E254D mutation (glutamate 254 substituted by aspartate) is expected to slow down GTP hydrolysis compared to wildtype microtubules.
source: To investigate how GTP hydrolysis determines conformational transformations within the GTP cap, we generated a human tubulin mutant, in which glutamate 254 is substituted by aspartate (E254D) (Figure 3a). This chemically similar but shorter catalytic residue is expected to slow down GTP hydrolysis compared to wildtype microtubules.
evidence: The claim is based on the chemical properties of the amino acid substitution and is a prediction.

claim: E254D microtubules grow steadily from surface-immobilized seeds.
source: E254D microtubules grew steadily from surface-immobilized seeds (Figure 3b)
evidence: The claim is supported by iSCAT microscopy data shown in Figure 3b.

claim: EB3 tracks the growing ends of E254D microtubules, displaying strikingly longer and brighter fluorescent 'comets' than on wildtype microtubules.
source: and EB3 tracked their growing ends, displaying strikingly longer and brighter fluorescent 'comets' (Figure 3c–d, Videos 5–7), clearly indicative of slower GTP hydrolysis.
evidence: The claim is supported by TIRF microscopy data shown in Figure 3c-d and Videos 5-7.

claim: E254D microtubules hardly ever display catastrophes even under conditions where wildtype microtubules exhibit frequent depolymerization events.
source: E254D microtubules hardly ever displayed any catastrophes even under conditions where wildtype microtubules exhibited frequent depolymerization events (Figure 3e–f, Videos 5–7).
evidence: The claim is supported by TIRF microscopy data shown in Figure 3e-f and Videos 5-7.

claim: E254D tubulin nucleates microtubules more efficiently in solution than wildtype tubulin, but less than E254A tubulin.
source: E254D tubulin also nucleated microtubules more efficiently in solution than wildtype tubulin, but less than E254A tubulin (Figure 3b, Figure 1h) indicating an intermediate stability of E254D microtubules compared to wildtype and completely GTPase-deficient E254A microtubules.
evidence: The claim is supported by iSCAT microscopy data shown in Figure 3b and Figure 1h.

claim: GTP hydrolysis is slowed down in the E254D mutant.
source: This suggests that GTP hydrolysis is indeed slowed down in the E254D mutant.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the nucleation and stability data of E254D microtubules.

claim: E254D microtubules grow about twofold faster than wildtype microtubules, either with or without EB3.
source: E254D microtubules grew about twofold faster than wildtype microtubules, either with or without EB3 (Figure 3h).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 3h.

claim: Around 5 times more EB3 binds to the ends of E254D microtubules compared to wildtype microtubules growing at comparable speeds.
source: A comparison of the average EB3 intensity profiles along the ends of wildtype and E254D microtubules growing at tubulin concentrations adjusted such that they grow with comparable speeds, shows that around ~5 times more EB3 binds to the ends of E254D microtubules (Figure 3i).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 3i.

claim: The increase in EB3 binding to E254D microtubules can to a large extent be explained by the longer EB3 binding region on the mutant microtubules.
source: This increase can to a large extent be explained by the longer EB3 binding region on the mutant microtubules (Figure 3j).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 3j.

claim: The lifetime of the EB3 binding region is four-fold longer at the ends of E254D microtubules compared to wildtype microtubules.
source: Quantitative analysis of the intensity profiles allows to extract the characteristic comet lengths and, knowing the measured growth speeds, also the lifetime of the EB3 binding region (Bieling et al., 2008; Bieling et al., 2007; Maurer et al., 2014; Maurer et al., 2012), which was four-fold longer at the ends of E254D microtubules compared to wildtype microtubules (Figure 3j).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 3j and by citations to prior methods.

claim: Slowed-down GTP hydrolysis extends the lifetime and hence the size of the GTP cap.
source: These results demonstrate that slowed-down GTP hydrolysis extends the lifetime and hence the size of the GTP cap.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the experimental data on E254D microtubules.

claim: Split comets at the growing ends of E254D microtubules indicate that even partial microtubule end structures can be more stable when GTP hydrolysis is slow.
source: We occasionally observed 'split comets' at the growing ends of E254D microtubules that could later re-join (Figure 3g, magenta arrowheads) or detach and grow individually (Figure 3g, cyan arrowheads). This indicates that even partial microtubule end structures can be more stable when GTP hydrolysis is slow.
evidence: The claim is supported by TIRF microscopy data shown in Figure 3g and by inference from the observation.

claim: The 'curved' appearance of partial comets likely reflects global conformational differences between unfinished end structures and fully formed tubes, pointing to a high degree of structural plasticity of the GTP cap region.
source: The 'curved' appearance of these partial comets likely reflects global conformational differences between unfinished end structures such as observed for microtubule nucleation and fully formed tubes, pointing to a high degree of structural plasticity of the GTP cap region (Roostalu and Surrey, 2017; Voter and Erickson, 1984; Brouhard and Rice, 2018; Igaev and Grubmüller, 2018).
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the observation of split comets and is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: An overall complex (non-mono-exponential) distribution of mGFP-EB3 dwell times in the GTP cap is indicative of the presence of different conformational states with different EB3 binding affinities in the cap.
source: We observed an overall complex (non-mono-exponential) distribution of mGFP-EB3 dwell times in the GTP cap, indicative of the presence of different conformational states with different EB3 binding affinities in the cap (Figure 4b).
evidence: The claim is supported by single molecule dwell time analysis shown in Figure 4b.

claim: Local dwell time distributions at distinct distances from the growing microtubule end are rather mono-exponential, indicative of a more homogenous local conformational lattice state.
source: Next, we performed a spatially resolved dwell time analysis by generating several 'local dwell time distributions' for distinct distances from the growing microtubule end. These local distributions were rather mono-exponential, indicative of a more homogenous local conformational lattice state (Figure 4c).
evidence: The claim is supported by spatially resolved dwell time analysis shown in Figure 4c.

claim: The local characteristic EB3 dwell times decrease along the length of the GTP cap.
source: The local characteristic EB3 dwell times decreased along the length of the GTP cap (Figure 4c–d, Figure 4—figure supplement 2a).
evidence: The claim is supported by spatially resolved dwell time analysis shown in Figure 4c-d and Figure 4—figure supplement 2a.

claim: A decreasing EB binding affinity along the length of the GTP cap suggests a gradual conformational change within the cap.
source: This indicates a decreasing EB binding affinity along the length of the GTP cap, suggesting a gradual conformational change within the cap.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the dwell time data.

claim: The long EB3 dwell times at the very tip of the GTP cap are indicative of a GTP-like state.
source: The long EB3 dwell times at the very tip of the GTP cap are indicative of a GTP-like state, given that EB3 binds strongly to GTPase deficient E254A microtubules (Figure 2f–k), which then transforms into the lower affinity GDP state concomitant with GTP hydrolysis.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the dwell time data and comparison to E254A microtubules.

claim: The conformational change along the length of the GTP cap most likely reflects a stability gradient whose characteristic length corresponds to the cap length.
source: The conformational change along the length of the GTP cap most likely reflects a stability gradient whose characteristic length corresponds to the cap length (Figure 4d).
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the dwell time data shown in Figure 4d.

claim: A similar gradual conformational change is observed in the shorter GTP caps of wildtype microtubules growing at a similar speed to E254D microtubules.
source: We observed a similar gradual conformational change in the shorter GTP caps of wildtype microtubules growing at a similar speed (Figure 4—figure supplement 3), when we recorded a considerably larger number of single molecule binding events compared to previous studies (Bieling et al., 2008; Bieling et al., 2007; Dixit et al., 2009; Maurer et al., 2011; Maurer et al., 2014) to enable spatially resolved dwell time analysis (Figure 4e–h).
evidence: The claim is supported by single molecule dwell time analysis shown in Figure 4e-h and Figure 4—figure supplement 3, and by citations to prior work.

claim: A combination of conformational states is detected within the whole GTP cap of wildtype microtubules, as indicated by a complex EB3 dwell time distribution for all events observed in the entire cap region.
source: We detected also here a combination of conformational states within the whole GTP cap, as indicated by a complex EB3 dwell time distribution for all events observed in the entire cap region (Figure 4f)
evidence: The claim is supported by dwell time analysis shown in Figure 4f.

claim: Rather homogenous conformational states are detected at distinct positions within the wildtype GTP cap, as indicated by more mono-exponential local dwell time distributions.
source: whereas rather homogenous conformational states were detected at distinct positions within the GTP cap, as indicated by more mono-exponential local dwell time distributions (Figure 4g).
evidence: The claim is supported by spatially resolved dwell time analysis shown in Figure 4g.

claim: The mean dwell times decrease over a shorter distance in wildtype GTP caps than in E254D caps, reflecting the shorter EB3 comet length at wildtype microtubule ends.
source: The mean dwell times, indicative of the EB3 binding affinity, decreased over a shorter distance in wildtype GTP caps (Figure 4h, Figure 4—figure supplement 2c) than in E254D caps (Figure 4d, Figure 4—figure supplement 2a), reflecting the shorter EB3 comet length at wildtype microtubule ends compared to longer EB3 comets at E254D microtubule ends with reduced GTPase activity (Figure 3j, Figure 4—figure supplement 2b,d).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of dwell time data shown in Figure 4h, Figure 4d, and Figure 4—figure supplement 2, and comet data in Figure 3j.

claim: A conformational gradient in the GTP cap at the growing microtubule end is a response to the GTP hydrolysis in the lattice.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that a conformational gradient in the GTP cap at the growing microtubule end is a response to the GTP hydrolysis in the lattice.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the experimental data on dwell times and conformational changes.

claim: GTP-microtubules produced using recombinant mutated human tubulin were hyper-stable, as predicted by the GTP cap hypothesis.
source: Using recombinant mutated human tubulin we produced for the first time pure GTP-microtubules, eliminating the need for using non-hydrolysable GTP analogues. GTP-microtubules were hyper-stable, as predicted by the GTP cap hypothesis
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data on E254A microtubules and by reference to the GTP cap hypothesis.

claim: EBs bind strongly to GTP microtubules.
source: and EBs bound strongly to these GTP microtubules.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data on EB3 binding to E254A microtubules.

claim: Microtubules with impaired GTP hydrolysis (E254D) are more stable than wildtype microtubules and display higher nucleation efficiency.
source: Microtubules with impaired, but not blocked GTPase rate were also considerably more stable than wildtype microtubules and displayed higher nucleation efficiency.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data on E254D microtubules.

claim: Microtubules with impaired GTP hydrolysis (E254D) display longer EB comets, indicative of slowed-down GTP hydrolysis.
source: They had an elongated EB binding region at the growing microtubule ends, indicative of slowed-down GTP hydrolysis.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data on EB3 comets on E254D microtubules.

claim: The kinetics of GTP hydrolysis determine GTP cap length.
source: Our results are to date the most direct demonstration that the kinetics of GTP hydrolysis determine GTP cap length
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the experimental data on wildtype, E254A, and E254D microtubules.

claim: EBs bind to the GTP cap.
source: and that EBs bind to the GTP cap, explaining why their binding region represents the part of the microtubule that stabilizes it (Duellberg et al., 2016; Maurer et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data on EB3 binding and by citations to prior work.

claim: The length of the GTP cap of recombinant human wildtype microtubules is in a similar range as previously measured EB 'comet' lengths with mammalian brain microtubules in vitro and in cells.
source: The length of the GTP cap of recombinant human wildtype microtubules was in a similar range as previously measured EB 'comet' lengths with mammalian brain microtubules in vitro (Bieling et al., 2008; Bieling et al., 2007; Dixit et al., 2009; Maurer et al., 2011; Rickman et al., 2017; Roth et al., 2018; Vemu et al., 2017) and in cells (Seetapun et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of experimental data with prior published work.

claim: Recombinant human wildtype tubulin and mammalian brain tubulin hydrolyze GTP with similar speeds.
source: This confirms that recombinant human wildtype tubulin and mammalian brain tubulin hydrolyze GTP with similar speeds (Vemu et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the comparison of GTP cap lengths and is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The hydrolysis rate appears to be set such that sufficiently long GTP caps are created to stabilize growing microtubules during fluctuating growth.
source: The hydrolysis rate appears to be set such that sufficiently long GTP caps are created to stabilize growing microtubules during fluctuating growth (Duellberg et al., 2016; Gardner et al., 2011; Rickman et al., 2017; Schek et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is an inference supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Neither GMPCPP nor GTPγS generate microtubules with properties identical to microtubules that contain GTP.
source: Our results suggest that previous observations with GTP analogues require careful interpretation, because neither GMPCPP nor GTPγS generate microtubules with properties identical to microtubules that contain GTP.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the experimental data comparing E254A microtubules with GMPCPP and GTPγS microtubules.

claim: Each GTP analogue (GMPCPP and GTPγS) produces some, but not all features of the microtubule lattice conformation in the GTP cap when considering microtubule stability and the affinity for EB binding.
source: When considering microtubule stability and the affinity for EB binding, each analogue appears to produce some, but not all features of the microtubule lattice conformation in the GTP cap.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the experimental data.

claim: The observed short EB-free zone at the extreme microtubule end is probably a consequence of finite EB association kinetics and of some particular structural feature at the very end of growing microtubules.
source: The recent observation of a short EB-free region at the very end of growing microtubules (Maurer et al., 2014) together with the observation of EBs not binding GMPCPP very well, had stimulated a discussion about the possibility of EBs binding a post-hydrolysis and not a GTP induced conformation of the microtubule lattice (Maurer et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2015). Given the results presented here, this can now be considered unlikely. The observed short EB-free zone at the extreme microtubule end is probably rather a consequence of finite EB association kinetics (Maurer et al., 2014) and of some particular structural feature at the very end of growing microtubules.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the experimental data and is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: EB binding sites that are located between protofilaments may not form at the very microtubule end due to a flared growing microtubule end structure lacking lateral protofilaments interactions, or another GTP lattice conformation may exist at the very microtubule end.
source: EB binding sites that are located between protofilaments (Maurer et al., 2012; Zhang et al., 2015), may not form there due to a flared growing microtubule end structure lacking lateral protofilaments interactions, as observed recently (McIntosh et al., 2018), or another GTP lattice conformation may exist at the very microtubule end.
evidence: The claim is speculation supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The binding strength of EB3 decreases gradually from the microtubule end towards the GDP lattice for both wildtype and E254D caps.
source: The binding strength of EB3 decreased gradually from the microtubule end towards the GDP lattice (Figure 4d,h), both for wildtype and E254D caps.
evidence: The claim is supported by spatially resolved dwell time analysis shown in Figure 4d and 4h.

claim: Binding strength of EB3 decays mono-exponentially on a length scale similar to the comet lengths measured by 'comet' analysis.
source: Binding strength decayed mono-exponentially on a length scale similar to the comet lengths measured by 'comet' analysis (Figure 3j), suggesting that the density of EBs decreases along the length of the cap due to an affinity decrease.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of dwell time data with comet analysis data shown in Figure 3j.

claim: The time scale of the affinity decrease as the microtubule grows provides an estimate for the GTP hydrolysis rate which is approximately 0.2 s−1 for wildtype microtubules and four times slower for E254D microtubules.
source: The associated time scale of this affinity decrease as the microtubule grows provides an estimate for the GTP hydrolysis rate which is ~0.2 s−1 for wildtype microtubules and four times slower for E254D microtubules.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the dwell time and growth speed data.

claim: EB3 diffuses on the microtubule lattice with a diffusion coefficient of approximately 10−3 µm2/s.
source: Using a mean squared displacement (MSD) analysis of single EB3 molecules bound to E254D caps we find that EB3 diffuses on the microtubule lattice with a diffusion coefficient of ~10−3 µm2/s.
evidence: The claim is supported by MSD analysis of single molecule data.

claim: During a typical binding event EB3 samples the conformational state of several tubulins in a range of up to approximately 50 nm.
source: Although this is several magnitudes slower than EB1 lattice diffusion reported previously under different conditions on microtubules grown in nucleotide analogues (Lopez and Valentine, 2016), it means that during a typical binding event EB3 samples the conformational state of several tubulins in a range of up to ~50 nm in our experiments.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the diffusion coefficient and is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The spatial resolution of EB3 as a conformational reporter is approximately 50 nm.
source: This defines the spatial resolution of this conformational reporter.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the diffusion analysis.

claim: EBs clearly detect a conformational gradient within the GTP cap, as evidenced by the dependence of its mean dwell time on the distance from the growing microtubule end.
source: Nevertheless, EBs clearly detect a conformational gradient within the GTP cap, as evidenced by the dependence of its mean dwell time on the distance from the growing microtubule end.
evidence: The claim is supported by the spatially resolved dwell time data.

claim: The ratio between the dwell times of EB3 bound to E254A microtubules versus wildtype microtubule ends is considerably larger than the ratio between the corresponding equilibrium association constants.
source: Interestingly, the ratio between the dwell times of EB3 bound to E254A microtubules (Figure 2h–i, Figure 2—figure supplement 1f,g) versus wildtype microtubule ends (Figure 4f) was considerably larger than the ratio between the corresponding equilibrium association constants (inverse equilibrium dissociation constants) (Figure 2d and i).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of dwell time and affinity data shown in the referenced figures.

claim: Not only the unbinding rate, but also the binding rate of EB3 is reduced on E254A microtubules compared to wildtype microtubules.
source: This indicates that not only the unbinding rate, but also the binding rate of EB3 is reduced on E254A microtubules compared to wildtype microtubules, even if so to a lesser extent.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the comparison of dwell times and equilibrium constants.

claim: EB3 may induce and stabilize a conformational lattice transformation in E254A microtubules when it binds, akin to an 'induced fit' scenario.
source: This suggests that EB3 may induce and stabilize a conformational lattice transformation in E254A microtubules when it binds, akin to an 'induced fit' scenario.
evidence: The claim is speculation based on the kinetic data.

claim: EB binding to microtubules can change their protofilament twist.
source: Such an effect on the microtubule lattice would agree with previous observations showing that EB binding to microtubules can change their protofilament twist (von Loeffelholz et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2018)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior published work.

claim: EB binding mildly accelerates cap maturation, which means 'accelerate GTP hydrolysis'.
source: and mildly accelerate cap maturation (Maurer et al., 2011). We can now conclude that the latter means 'accelerate GTP hydrolysis', in agreement with our results here as well as recent structural observations (Zhang et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the experimental data and is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The kinetics of GTP hydrolysis critically determine the properties of the GTP cap the size of which can be monitored by EBs.
source: In conclusion, our results demonstrate that the kinetics of GTP hydrolysis critically determine the properties of the GTP cap the size of which can be monitored by EBs.
evidence: The claim is a summary inference drawn from all the experimental data.

claim: EBs serve as a binding platform for numerous microtubule binding proteins, ensuring that microtubule dynamics in cells is regulated at multiple levels by targeting the GTP cap.
source: Because EBs serve as a binding platform for numerous microtubule binding proteins it ensures that microtubule dynamics in cells is regulated at multiple levels by targeting the most critical modulator of microtubule stability, the GTP cap, itself.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on established knowledge about EB function.

claim: Growing microtubules are thought to be stabilized by a GTP cap at their ends.
source: Growing microtubules are thought to be stabilized by a GTP cap at their ends.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge.

claim: The nature of the GTP cap is still poorly understood.
source: The nature of this cap, however, is still poorly understood.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge.

claim: End Binding proteins (EBs) recruit a diverse range of regulators of microtubule function to growing microtubule ends.
source: End Binding proteins (EBs) recruit a diverse range of regulators of microtubule function to growing microtubule ends.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge.

claim: Whether the EB binding region is identical to the GTP cap is unclear.
source: Whether the EB binding region is identical to the GTP cap is unclear.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about the state of the field.

claim: Slowing-down GTP hydrolysis leads to extended GTP caps.
source: Slowing-down GTP hydrolysis leads to extended GTP caps.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data on E254D microtubules.

claim: Cap length determines microtubule stability.
source: We find that cap length determines microtubule stability
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data comparing wildtype, E254A, and E254D microtubules.

claim: The microtubule conformation changes gradually in the cap as GTP is hydrolyzed.
source: and that the microtubule conformation changes gradually in the cap as GTP is hydrolyzed.
evidence: The claim is supported by spatially resolved dwell time analysis.

claim: The GTP cap coincides with the EB-binding region.
source: These results demonstrate the critical importance of the kinetics of GTP hydrolysis for microtubule stability and establish that the GTP cap coincides with the EB-binding region.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from all the experimental data.

claim: Microtubules are hollow tubes that polymerize by the addition of GTP-bound α/β-tubulin heterodimers to their ends.
source: Microtubules are hollow tubes that polymerize by the addition of GTP-bound α/β-tubulin heterodimers to their ends.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge.

claim: Tubulin incorporation induces GTP hydrolysis which destabilizes the microtubule wall.
source: Tubulin incorporation induces GTP hydrolysis which destabilizes the microtubule wall.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge.

claim: A delay in hydrolysis of unknown duration is thought to produce a 'GTP cap', a protective end structure formed of GTP-tubulins that is critical for microtubule stability.
